A pup is simply a young dog. It means exactly the same thing as "puppy" — just a shorter, slightly more informal way of saying it. When a dog gives birth, the babies are called pups. They are small, dependent on their mother, and not yet fully grown.

"The dog gave birth to six pups."

Here is where it gets more interesting. In English, "pup" is not limited to dogs. It is also used to describe the young of several other animals, especially mammals. The animals whose young are commonly called pups include:

  • Seals and sea lions — this is one of the most frequent uses outside of dogs
  • Sharks
  • Rats and mice
  • Wolves
  • Otters
  • Foxes
  • Minks

What these animals share is that their young are born small and helpless, needing care — much like a puppy does. So when you hear or read "a seal pup," it simply means a baby seal.

"Pup" is also used informally to describe a young, inexperienced person, especially one who acts a little too confident or bold for their age or experience. It carries a mild sense of "you are young and still have a lot to learn."

"Listen here, pup — I've been doing this job for thirty years."

This usage is often said by an older person to a younger one, in a tone that is somewhere between affectionate and mildly dismissive. It is not usually a harsh insult — more of a gentle reminder that someone is still new to something.

1. "In pup"
When a female dog (or similar animal) is pregnant and carrying unborn young inside her, she is described as being "in pup."

"We can't take her to the show — she's in pup."

2. "Sold a pup"
This is a common British English idiom. To be "sold a pup" means to be cheated or deceived — to pay for something and receive something far worse than what was promised, or to be tricked into a bad deal altogether.

"He paid a lot of money for that car, but it broke down the next day. He was sold a pup."

The phrase comes from an old practice where dishonest sellers would trick buyers into thinking they were buying a fully grown, valuable dog, but instead hand over a young pup of much less value.
The Subtle Feeling of the Word

Compared to "puppy," the word "pup" feels slightly more grown-up and practical. "Puppy" sounds cute and soft; "pup" sounds direct and natural. A wildlife documentary is more likely to say "seal pup" than "seal puppy." A farmer or breeder is just as likely to say "pup" as "puppy." Both are correct when talking about a young dog — it simply comes down to context and personal preference.

SituationWhat "pup" means

In short: pup most fundamentally means a young dog. By extension, it refers to the young of several other mammals. When used about a person, it gently suggests youth and inexperience. The phrase "in pup" means pregnant, and "sold a pup" means cheated. That covers everything the word does.
